questions.text: Lightning heats the air around it to roughly thirty thousand degrees Celsius, about five times the temperature of the surface of the sun. The air expands so violently that it produces the shock wave we hear as thunder. Because light travels far faster than sound, counting the seconds between the flash and the rumble gives a rough measure of distance.

zh.Lightning heats the air around it to rou: 閃電會把周圍的空氣加熱到大約攝氏三萬度，約是太陽表面溫度的五倍。空氣劇烈膨脹，產生我們聽到的衝擊波，也就是雷聲。由於光的傳播速度遠比聲音快，計算閃光與雷聲之間相隔的秒數，就能粗略估算出距離。

questions.text: Silk is produced by caterpillars that spin a single continuous thread to build a cocoon. A single cocoon can yield nearly a kilometre of fibre, which is why the material was once worth more than gold by weight. For centuries the method was a closely guarded secret, and revealing it was punishable by death.

zh.Silk is produced by caterpillars that sp: 蠶絲是由毛毛蟲吐出一條連續不斷的絲線來結繭所產生的。一個蠶繭可以抽出將近一公里長的纖維，這就是為什麼這種材料以重量計算曾經比黃金還貴。好幾個世紀以來，這種方法都是嚴加保守的秘密，洩漏出去甚至可能被處死。

questions.text: Braille was invented by a fifteen-year-old student who had lost his sight in a childhood accident. He adapted a military code of raised dots, reducing it to six positions that a fingertip can read without moving. Schools resisted the system for decades, partly because sighted teachers found it difficult to learn.

zh.Braille was invented by a fifteen-year-o: 點字是由一位在童年意外中失明的十五歲學生發明的。他改造了一種以凸點構成的軍用密碼，把它簡化為六個位置，讓指尖不必移動就能讀取。學校抗拒這套系統長達數十年，部分原因是明眼的老師覺得很難學會。

questions.text: Scurvy killed more sailors than storms or battle until the eighteenth century, when a naval surgeon showed that citrus fruit could prevent it. His trial compared six treatments on twelve sick men and is often described as the first controlled clinical experiment. Even so, the navy took more than forty years to act on the result.

zh.Scurvy killed more sailors than storms o: 在十八世紀之前，壞血病奪走的水手性命比風暴或戰鬥還多，直到一位海軍外科醫師證明柑橘類水果可以預防它。他的試驗在十二名病人身上比較了六種療法，常被稱為第一個對照臨床實驗。即便如此，海軍仍花了四十多年才根據這個結果採取行動。

questions.text: The earliest photographs required exposures of several hours, which is why the first street scenes appear deserted. Anyone walking past simply vanished, while a man having his shoes polished stood still long enough to be recorded. Within two decades, faster chemistry had cut exposures to a fraction of a second.

zh.The earliest photographs required exposu: 最早的照片需要曝光好幾個小時，這就是為什麼最初的街景照看起來空無一人。任何路過的人都直接消失了，而一名正在擦鞋的男子因為站得夠久，才被記錄下來。不到二十年，更快的化學技術就把曝光時間縮短到不到一秒。

questions.text: Peatlands cover only about three per cent of the land surface, yet they store twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests combined. The carbon accumulates because waterlogged ground slows decay to a crawl. When peat is drained for farming, that ancient store begins to break down and escapes into the atmosphere.

zh.Peatlands cover only about three per cen: 泥炭地只覆蓋約百分之三的陸地表面，儲存的碳卻是全世界森林總和的兩倍。碳之所以會累積，是因為浸水的土地讓分解變得極為緩慢。當泥炭地為了耕作而被排乾時，這個古老的碳庫就會開始分解，並逸散到大氣中。

questions.text: Why is it so easy to forget someone’s name a moment after hearing it? The answer has little to do with a failing memory and a great deal to do with attention. A name is an arbitrary label: it carries no meaning that can be attached to anything else you know about the person. Faces, by contrast, connect to a rich network of information, which is why we recognise a face while groping for the name. Most of the time, the name was never properly encoded, because in the seconds after an introduction we are usually thinking about what to say next. The practical remedies follow from this. Repeat the name aloud once, use it within the first minute, and link it deliberately to something you already know, such as another person with the same name. None of these tricks improves your memory; they simply ensure that the name gets into it in the first place.

the name is often never encoded, because we are thinking about what to say

questions.text: The second-hand clothing trade is far larger than most people realise. When you donate a bag of clothes to a charity shop in Europe, only a small proportion is sold locally. As fast fashion has driven down the durability of garments, a growing share of each bale is unsellable on arrival, and the receiving country is left with the cost of disposal. questions.text: People have farmed on the slopes of active volcanoes for thousands of years, which looks reckless until you look at the soil. Volcanic ash weathers into some of the most fertile ground on Earth. It is rich in phosphorus, potassium and trace minerals, and its porous structure holds water while still draining well. In parts of Indonesia and Italy, land within a few kilometres of a crater supports several harvests a year, and population density around some volcanoes is far higher than in the surrounding regions. The trade-off is obvious but unevenly understood. Major eruptions are rare enough that a family may farm for three generations without seeing one, and the memory of the last event fades faster than the fertility does. Modern monitoring has improved warning times considerably, but evacuation still depends on people being willing to leave land that has, in every year of living memory, simply made them prosperous.

questions.title: Should the city introduce a congestion charge?

turns.text: I support a congestion charge for the city centre. Traffic has grown every year, buses are stuck in it, and the cities that have tried it, London and Stockholm, saw traffic fall by around twenty per cent almost immediately.

My concern is who pays. A flat daily charge is nothing to someone in a company car and a real cost to a cleaner driving in for a six o’clock shift when no buses run. It is a tax that falls hardest on the people with the fewest alternatives.

That is the strongest objection, but it is an argument about design rather than about the charge itself. Stockholm exempted some vehicles and spent the revenue on suburban transport, which made the scheme popular enough to survive a referendum.
So the money has to be visibly spent on alternatives, not absorbed into the general budget.
If it funded night buses and a discount for shift workers, I could support it. Without that, I think it just prices poorer drivers off the road.
Then we should also publish the traffic and air quality data each year, so the promise can actually be checked.

questions.title: Should employers monitor staff with software?

turns.text: Since we moved to hybrid working, our company installed software that records active hours and screenshots. Management says it is about fairness, so that people carrying the load are recognised. I think that is a reasonable aim.

The aim may be reasonable, but the measure is not. What the software records is activity, not output. The people it flags are often those doing the thinking, and the people it rewards are the ones who have learned to keep the mouse moving.

There is also evidence that monitoring changes behaviour in unhelpful ways. Studies of monitored call centres find that staff hit their targets and stop doing the small favours for colleagues that nobody measures.
So you would rather managers judged by results, even though results are harder to measure?
Yes, because harder to measure is not the same as impossible. Agree what a good month looks like, and review it.
And if any monitoring stays, staff should see exactly what is collected about them. Secret measurement destroys trust faster than any productivity gain can repay.

questions.title: Measuring inflation
questions.passage:
Inflation sounds like a simple idea: the rate at which prices rise. Measuring it is far harder than it appears. Statistical agencies track the price of a basket of goods and services meant to represent what a typical household buys, and the composition of that basket determines the answer. Because spending patterns change, the basket must be revised regularly, and each revision involves judgement.

Two problems are particularly stubborn. The first is quality. A laptop that costs the same as one sold five years ago is a far better machine, so part of the price reflects more product rather than inflation, and agencies must estimate how much. The second is substitution. When beef becomes expensive, households buy more chicken, so a fixed basket overstates the rise in their actual cost of living.

These are not academic concerns. Pensions, wages and welfare payments are often linked to the published figure, so a small bias moves large sums of money. They also explain why people sometimes insist that inflation is higher than the official rate: the index describes an average household that resembles nobody exactly, and it gives no extra weight to the items, such as rent or food, that people notice most.
questions.model: Although inflation appears simple, measuring it depends on the composition of a regularly revised basket of goods and on difficult judgements about improving quality and about substitution between products, which matters because pensions and wages are linked to the published figure and because the average it describes matches no individual household.

questions.title: The other carbon problem
questions.passage:
About a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by human activity does not stay in the atmosphere. It dissolves into the ocean, where it reacts with seawater to form carbonic acid. Since the industrial revolution, this process has made the surface ocean around thirty per cent more acidic, a change that is happening faster than at any time in the past fifty million years.

The consequences fall hardest on organisms that build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate: corals, oysters, mussels and the tiny sea snails that underpin many polar food webs. As acidity rises, the carbonate these animals need becomes harder to obtain, and in the most affected waters existing shells begin to dissolve. Oyster hatcheries on the Pacific coast of North America have already had to treat incoming seawater to keep young shellfish alive.

Unlike warming, acidification cannot be moderated by any conceivable local measure, because the chemistry follows directly from the amount of carbon dioxide in the air. Scientists sometimes call it the other carbon problem, and note that it will continue even if the climate response to emissions turns out to be milder than expected.
questions.model: Because the ocean absorbs about a quarter of human carbon dioxide emissions, it has become roughly thirty per cent more acidic since the industrial revolution, which makes shell-building difficult for corals and shellfish and cannot be addressed locally, since the chemistry depends directly on carbon dioxide in the air.

zh.About a quarter of the carbon dioxide re: 人類活動排放的二氧化碳中，約有四分之一並沒有留在大氣中。它會溶入海洋，與海水反應形成碳酸。自工業革命以來，這個過程使表層海水的酸度提高了約百分之三十，而這個變化的速度比過去五千萬年間的任何時候都快。
zh.The consequences fall hardest on organis: 受影響最深的，是那些用碳酸鈣構築外殼和骨骼的生物：珊瑚、牡蠣、貽貝，以及支撐許多極地食物網的微小海螺。隨著酸度上升，這些動物所需的碳酸鹽變得更難取得，而在受影響最嚴重的水域，既有的外殼甚至開始溶解。北美太平洋沿岸的牡蠣孵化場，已經必須處理引入的海水，才能讓幼貝存活。
zh.Unlike warming, acidification cannot be: 與暖化不同，海洋酸化無法透過任何可想見的地方性措施來緩解，因為其化學反應直接取決於空氣中二氧化碳的含量。科學家有時稱它為「另一個碳問題」，並指出即使氣候對排放的反應比預期溫和，酸化仍會持續下去。
zh.Because the ocean absorbs about a quarte: 由於海洋吸收了人類約四分之一的二氧化碳排放，自工業革命以來其酸度已上升約百分之三十，使珊瑚和貝類難以形成外殼；而且由於這個化學過程直接取決於空氣中的二氧化碳，它無法以地方性措施解決。

questions.prompt: Some people think that all students should continue to study a science subject until they leave school, even if they have no interest in it. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
plan: Give your position in the introduction and say how strongly you hold it.
Arguments for: scientific literacy for voting and health decisions, and keeping options open.
Arguments against: time taken from subjects a student is committed to, and the risk of disengagement.
Distinguish between compulsory science and compulsory examinations in science.
Conclusion: restate your position and the condition that makes it work.

zh.Some people think that all students shou: 有些人認為，所有學生在畢業之前都應該持續修讀一門科學科目，即使他們對它毫無興趣。你在多大程度上同意或不同意這個說法？
zh.Give your position in the introduction a: 在引言中表明立場，並說明你支持的程度。
zh.Arguments for: scientific literacy for v: 支持的論點：投票與健康決策所需的科學素養，以及保留未來的選擇。
zh.Arguments against: time taken from subje: 反對的論點：占用學生真正投入的科目的時間，以及學生可能因此失去學習動力。
zh.Distinguish between compulsory science a: 區分「必修科學」與「科學必考」這兩件事。
zh.Conclusion: restate your position and th: 結論：重申你的立場，以及讓它可行的條件。

questions.title: The Gulf Stream
parts: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico towards north-west Europe, which is why Britain has milder winters than places at the same
. The current is part of a larger circulation driven by differences in temperature and salt, and it
on cold, salty water sinking in the far north. Meltwater from Greenland makes the surface fresher and therefore less dense, which could
that sinking. Most models suggest a gradual weakening rather than a sudden collapse, but the
of the estimates is itself a reason for concern.
why: Places compared for winter temperature are at the same latitude, the north–south position that governs climate. Longitude runs east–west and would not explain milder winters.
Collocation: a current depends on something. “insists” and “consists” need different prepositions, and “reflects on” means to think about.
Fresher, less dense water sinks less readily, so the meltwater could slow the sinking. “speed” would reverse the effect described.
The sentence contrasts a gradual weakening with the uncertainty around it, and the width of a range of estimates is how uncertainty is described.

zh.The Gulf Stream carries warm water from: 墨西哥灣流把溫暖的海水從墨西哥灣帶往西北歐，這就是為什麼英國的冬天比同 ____ 的其他地方溫和。這股洋流是一個更大循環系統的一部分，由溫度和鹽度的差異所驅動，而它 ____ 於北方冰冷、高鹽度的海水下沉。來自格陵蘭的融水使表層海水鹽度降低、密度變小，這可能會 ____ 那樣的下沉。大多數模型顯示的是逐漸減弱而不是突然崩潰，但這些估計值的 ____ 本身就是令人擔憂的理由。
zh.Places compared for winter temperature a: 拿來比較冬季氣溫的地方位於相同的 latitude（緯度），也就是決定氣候的南北位置。longitude（經度）是東西向的，無法解釋為什麼冬天比較溫和。
zh.Collocation: a current depends on someth: 固定搭配：洋流 depends on（依賴）某事物。insists 和 consists 需要搭配不同的介系詞，而 reflects on 的意思是「思考」。
zh.Fresher, less dense water sinks less rea: 鹽度較低、密度較小的水比較不容易下沉，所以融水可能會 slow（減緩）下沉。speed 會把文中描述的效應顛倒過來。
zh.The sentence contrasts a gradual weakeni: 這句話把逐漸減弱與其中的不確定性加以對比，而估計範圍的 width（寬度）正是描述不確定性的方式。

questions.title: Reading in silence
parts: For most of recorded history, reading was done out loud. Ancient texts were written without spaces between words, so a reader had to sound them out in order to
where one word ended and the next began. Silent reading was rare enough that writers remarked on it with
. The introduction of word spacing by Irish and English scribes in the seventh century made it far easier to read with the eye
. That change did more than improve comfort: it allowed readers to move quickly through unfamiliar material, and it made the private,
relationship with a text that we now take for granted.
why: Sounding out unspaced text helps a reader work out, or tell, where each word ends. “speak” and “listen” do not take “where one word ended”.
Writers commented on silent reading because it was unusual, so they remarked on it with surprise. Approval or regret would not explain why it was worth remarking on at all.
“read with the eye alone” means without the voice. “only” cannot follow the noun in this way, and “lonely” describes a feeling.
The paragraph is about the change to silent reading, and a private, silent relationship with a text is what word spacing made possible.

zh.For most of recorded history, reading wa: 在有文字記載的大部分歷史中，閱讀都是出聲進行的。古代文本的字與字之間沒有空格，所以讀者必須把字音唸出來，才能 ____ 一個字在哪裡結束、下一個字從哪裡開始。默讀非常罕見，罕見到作家會帶著 ____ 提到它。七世紀愛爾蘭和英格蘭抄寫員引入字間空格之後，只用眼睛 ____ 閱讀就變得容易許多。這個改變帶來的不只是舒適：它讓讀者能快速讀過不熟悉的內容，也造就了我們今天視為理所當然、與文本之間那種私密而 ____ 的關係。
zh.Sounding out unspaced text helps a reade: 把沒有空格的文字唸出聲音，能幫助讀者判斷、也就是 tell（辨別）每個字在哪裡結束。speak 和 listen 都無法接「一個字在哪裡結束」。
zh.Writers commented on silent reading beca: 作家之所以會提到默讀，是因為它很不尋常，所以他們帶著 surprise（驚訝）提起它。approval 或 regret 都無法解釋為什麼這件事值得一提。
zh.“read with the eye alone” means without: read with the eye alone（只用眼睛閱讀）表示不出聲。only 不能這樣放在名詞後面，而 lonely 描述的是一種感受。
zh.The paragraph is about the change to sil: 這一段談的是轉向默讀的改變，而與文本之間私密而 silent（無聲）的關係，正是字間空格所促成的。

questions.title: How insurance works
parts: Insurance works by pooling risk. Each customer pays a premium that is small compared with the loss being insured against, and the company pays out to the few who actually suffer that
. The arrangement only functions if losses are largely

: a flood that damages ten thousand homes at once can overwhelm an insurer in a way that ten thousand separate house fires would not. Insurers therefore buy their own cover from reinsurers, spreading the risk across the world. Climate change complicates this model, because events once treated as rare are becoming both more frequent and more
why: The company pays the few who suffer the event being insured against, which the sentence has just called a loss. A premium is what customers pay in.
The contrast is between one flood hitting ten thousand homes together and ten thousand unrelated fires, so the model needs losses that are independent of each other.
A flood damaging many homes at once is the example of losses that arrive together, so the worry is that events are becoming more correlated as well as more frequent.

zh.Insurance works by pooling risk. Each cu: 保險的運作方式是把風險集中起來分攤。每位客戶支付的保費，相對於所投保的損失而言金額很小，而保險公司則賠付給少數真正遭受該 ____ 的人。這種安排只有在損失大致上彼此 ____ 時才行得通：一次淹沒一萬戶人家的洪水，可能讓保險公司難以承受，而一萬起各自獨立的住宅火災則不會。因此，保險公司會向再保險公司投保，把風險分散到全世界。氣候變遷使這套模式變得複雜，因為過去被視為罕見的事件，如今不僅越來越頻繁，也越來越 ____ 。
zh.The company pays the few who suffer the: 保險公司賠付給少數遭受所保事故的人，而這句話前面已經把它稱為 loss（損失）。premium（保費）是客戶繳交的錢。
zh.The contrast is between one flood hittin: 這裡的對比是一次洪水同時侵襲一萬戶人家，與一萬起互不相關的火災，所以這套模式需要的是彼此 independent（獨立）的損失。
zh.A flood damaging many homes at once is t: 一次洪水損害許多住宅，正是損失同時發生的例子，所以令人擔憂的是這類事件除了更頻繁之外，也變得更加 correlated（相關聯）。

questions.title: Hydrogen fuel
parts: Hydrogen burns without producing carbon dioxide, which makes it an appealing fuel, but almost all of it is currently
from natural gas in a process that releases large amounts of that same gas. Hydrogen made by splitting water with renewable electricity avoids this problem, although it remains
than the conventional kind. A further difficulty is storage: hydrogen has a high energy content by weight but a very low one by

, so it must be compressed or cooled to extremely low temperatures. For this reason, most analysts expect it to be used where batteries are impractical, such as in steelmaking and shipping, rather than as a general
for petrol.
why: The sentence describes how hydrogen is made today, from natural gas, so it is produced from it. “imported” and “burned” do not describe manufacture.
The contrast with “avoids this problem” needs a drawback, and cost is the standard one: it remains dearer. “cleaner” would not be a disadvantage.
The sentence contrasts energy “by weight” with the opposite measure, which is by volume, and explains why hydrogen must be compressed.
Being used only where batteries fail, rather than everywhere, makes it not a general replacement for petrol. A container or reminder makes no sense here.

zh.Hydrogen burns without producing carbon: 氫燃燒時不會產生二氧化碳，這使它成為一種有吸引力的燃料，但目前幾乎所有的氫都是以天然氣 ____ 的，而這個過程會釋放大量同樣的氣體。用再生能源電力分解水所製造的氫可以避免這個問題，不過它仍然比傳統方式製造的氫更 ____ 。另一個困難是儲存：氫以重量計的能量含量很高，但以 ____ 計卻非常低，所以必須加壓或冷卻到極低的溫度。因此，大多數分析師預期它會被用在電池不切實際的領域，例如煉鋼和航運，而不是全面 ____ 汽油。
zh.The sentence describes how hydrogen is m: 這句話描述的是今天氫的製造方式，也就是以天然氣 produced（製造）。imported 和 burned 都無法描述製造過程。
zh.The contrast with “avoids this problem”: 與「可以避免這個問題」形成對比，需要一個缺點，而成本是最典型的缺點：它仍然比較 dearer（昂貴）。cleaner 並不是缺點。
zh.The sentence contrasts energy “by weight: 這句話把「以重量計」的能量與相反的衡量方式對比，也就是以 volume（體積）計，並解釋了為什麼氫必須加壓。
zh.Being used only where batteries fail, ra: 只在電池行不通的地方使用、而不是到處使用，表示它不是汽油的全面 replacement（替代品）。container 或 reminder 在這裡都說不通。

questions.title: Better forecasts
parts: Weather forecasting has improved more than most people notice. A five-day forecast today is about as
as a one-day forecast was in 1980. Three developments explain the change. Satellites now supply continuous observations over oceans, where measurements were once almost entirely
. Computing power allows models to divide the atmosphere into far smaller boxes. And forecasters run the same model many times from slightly different starting points, which shows how
each prediction is rather than offering a single answer. Beyond about ten days, however, the atmosphere remains chaotic, and no increase in computing power will
that limit.
why: The comparison is about forecast quality across decades, so a five-day forecast is now as accurate as a one-day forecast then.
Satellites gave continuous observations over oceans, where data had previously been almost entirely absent. “routine” would mean there was no gap to fill.
Running a model many times from slightly different starts shows the confidence in a forecast, that is, how certain it is.
Chaos sets a hard limit that more computing cannot remove. You cannot “measure away” a limit, and “extend” would mean forecasts could go further.

zh.Weather forecasting has improved more th: 天氣預報的進步比大多數人察覺到的還要多。今天的五日預報，大約和 1980 年的一日預報一樣 ____ 。有三項發展可以解釋這個改變。衛星現在能持續觀測海洋，而過去那裡的觀測資料幾乎完全 ____ 。運算能力讓模型能把大氣切分成小得多的網格。而且預報人員會用略有不同的起始條件，把同一個模型跑很多次，這顯示出每個預測有多 ____ ，而不是只給出單一答案。然而，超過大約十天之後，大氣仍然是混沌的，再多的運算能力也無法 ____ 這個限制。
zh.The comparison is about forecast quality: 這裡比較的是數十年來預報的品質，所以今天的五日預報和當年的一日預報一樣 accurate（準確）。
zh.Satellites gave continuous observations: 衛星提供了海洋上的連續觀測，而那裡過去幾乎完全 absent（沒有）資料。routine 表示本來就沒有空缺需要填補。
zh.Running a model many times from slightly: 用略有不同的起始條件把模型跑很多次，顯示的是對預報的信心程度，也就是它有多 certain（確定）。
zh.Chaos sets a hard limit that more comput: 混沌設下了一個再多運算能力也無法 remove（消除）的硬限制。你無法「測量掉」一個限制，而 extend 則表示預報可以延伸得更遠。

questions.passage: Mangroves are among the few trees that can live in salt water, and they do so by a combination of filtering and excretion: some species block most of the salt at the root, while others push it out through their leaves, which can be seen glittering with crystals at low tide. Their tangled roots trap sediment, and over time this builds new land rather than simply holding the existing shore in place. The forests they form are now recognised as one of the most efficient carbon stores on the planet, holding several times as much carbon per hectare as tropical rainforest, most of it locked in waterlogged mud rather than in wood. They also shelter the young of many commercially important fish, which is why fishing communities often notice the loss of a mangrove belt before scientists record it. Despite this, mangroves have been cleared faster than most forest types, largely for shrimp ponds and coastal building. Replanting schemes have had mixed results: seedlings planted in the wrong tidal zone, or in areas where the flow of fresh water has been altered, frequently die within two years. Ecologists increasingly argue that restoring water flow and allowing natural regrowth produces better results than planting alone.
questions.q: Which of the following are stated in the passage?
o: Mangroves deal with salt in more than one way.
Mangrove mud stores more carbon per hectare than rainforest.
Mangrove loss is usually recorded by scientists before local fishers notice it.
Most mangrove clearance has been for timber.
Planting seedlings alone is often not enough to restore a mangrove forest.
why: Stated: some species block salt at the root and others excrete it through the leaves.
Stated: mangrove forests hold several times as much carbon per hectare as tropical rainforest.
The passage says the opposite, that fishing communities often notice the loss before scientists record it.
The passage gives shrimp ponds and coastal building as the main reasons, not timber.
Stated: seedlings often die within two years, and ecologists argue that restoring water flow works better than planting alone.

zh.Mangroves are among the few trees that c: 紅樹林是少數能在鹹水中生存的樹木之一，牠們靠著過濾與排出兩種方式並用來做到這點：有些種類在根部就擋住大部分鹽分，有些則把鹽從葉片排出，退潮時可以看到葉面上閃著鹽的結晶。牠們盤根錯節的根系會攔住泥沙，久而久之造出新的陸地，而不只是把原有的海岸固定住。牠們形成的森林如今被視為地球上效率最高的碳庫之一，每公頃儲存的碳是熱帶雨林的好幾倍，而且大部分鎖在浸水的泥中，而不是在木材裡。牠們也庇護許多具經濟價值魚類的幼魚，這就是為什麼漁村往往比科學家更早察覺一片紅樹林帶的消失。儘管如此，紅樹林被砍除的速度比大多數森林類型都快，主要是為了養蝦池和海岸開發。復育計畫的成效不一：種在錯誤潮間帶、或種在淡水流動已被改變的區域的樹苗，常常兩年內就死亡。生態學家越來越主張，恢復水流並讓森林自然再生，效果比單靠種樹更好。
zh.Which of the following are stated in the: 下列哪些內容在文章中有提到？
zh.Mangroves deal with salt in more than on: 紅樹林處理鹽分的方式不只一種。
zh.Mangrove mud stores more carbon per hect: 紅樹林的泥土每公頃儲存的碳比雨林還多。
zh.Mangrove loss is usually recorded by sci: 紅樹林的消失通常是科學家先記錄到，之後當地漁民才察覺。
zh.Most mangrove clearance has been for tim: 紅樹林大多是為了取得木材而被砍除。
zh.Planting seedlings alone is often not en: 單靠種植樹苗往往不足以復育一片紅樹林。
zh.Stated: some species block salt at the r: 文中有提到：有些種類在根部擋住鹽分，有些則透過葉片把鹽排出。
zh.Stated: mangrove forests hold several ti: 文中有提到：紅樹林每公頃儲存的碳是熱帶雨林的好幾倍。
zh.The passage says the opposite, that fish: 文章說的正好相反：漁村往往比科學家更早察覺紅樹林的消失。
zh.The passage gives shrimp ponds and coast: 文章把養蝦池和海岸開發列為主要原因，而不是木材。
zh.Stated: seedlings often die within two y: 文中有提到：樹苗常在兩年內死亡，而生態學家主張恢復水流比單靠種樹更有效。

questions.passage: City centres are routinely several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, an effect first described in London two hundred years ago and now measured in almost every large city. The causes are well understood. Dark roofs and asphalt absorb sunlight that vegetation would have reflected or used; buildings trap heat in narrow streets and release it slowly at night; and vehicles, air conditioners and industry add heat directly. The difference is therefore largest not at noon but a few hours after sunset, when open ground has cooled and the city has not. The consequences fall unevenly. Districts with the least tree cover tend to be the poorest, and during heatwaves they record the highest rates of illness and death. Air conditioning protects those who have it while making the street outside hotter, which has led some researchers to describe it as a private solution with a public cost. Remedies are not technically difficult: painting roofs white, planting street trees, and keeping parks and water channels open all measurably reduce peak temperatures, and trees do so while also providing shade at street level. The obstacles are mainly budgets and maintenance, since young street trees need watering for several years before they contribute much.
questions.q: Which of the following are stated in the passage?
o: The temperature gap between a city and its surroundings peaks in the early evening rather than at midday.
The urban heat island effect was first described in the last fifty years.
Areas with fewer trees tend to suffer more during heatwaves.
Air conditioning raises the temperature outside the buildings it cools.
Painting roofs white has been shown to have no measurable effect.
why: Stated: the difference is largest a few hours after sunset, when open ground has cooled and the city has not.
The passage says the effect was first described in London two hundred years ago.
Stated: districts with the least tree cover are usually the poorest and record the highest heatwave illness and death rates.
Stated: air conditioning protects those who have it while making the street outside hotter.
The passage lists white roofs among measures that measurably reduce peak temperatures.

zh.City centres are routinely several degre: 市中心的氣溫通常比周圍鄉間高上好幾度，這個現象兩百年前首次在倫敦被描述，如今幾乎每座大城市都測量得到。成因已經相當清楚。深色屋頂和柏油吸收了原本會被植物反射或利用的陽光；建築物把熱困在狹窄的街道中，並在夜間緩慢釋放；而車輛、冷氣和工業則直接增加熱量。因此，溫差最大的時候不是中午，而是日落後幾個小時，此時空曠的土地已經冷卻，城市卻還沒有。後果分布得並不平均。樹木覆蓋最少的區域往往也是最貧窮的區域，而在熱浪期間，這些地方的患病率和死亡率最高。冷氣保護了擁有它的人，同時卻讓外面的街道更熱，因此有些研究者形容它是一種由公眾付出代價的私人解方。補救措施在技術上並不困難：把屋頂漆成白色、種植行道樹、保留公園和水道，都能明顯降低高溫峰值，而樹木還能同時在街道層面提供遮蔭。主要的障礙在於預算和維護，因為年輕的行道樹需要澆水好幾年，才能發揮明顯作用。
zh.Which of the following are stated in the: 下列哪些內容在文章中有提到？

questions.passage: Why zebras are striped has been argued over for more than a century. Camouflage was the usual answer: at a distance, or in moving herds, the pattern was said to confuse a lion. Tests of that idea have not gone well. Lions hunt largely at night and see poorly by day, and computer models of predator vision suggest the stripes are visible at closer range than a plain coat would be. A second theory, that the pattern helps zebras recognise each other, does not explain why other grazing animals manage without it. The strongest current evidence concerns flies. Biting flies carry disease, and across Africa the striping of zebra populations matches the distribution of those flies more closely than it matches temperature, predator numbers or herd size. Field experiments have since shown that horses wearing striped coats are approached by flies as often as plain horses but land on them far less: the flies fail to slow down properly and simply bump into the animal. That does not prove the flies drove the pattern's evolution, but it does explain the striping better than the older accounts do.
questions.q: What is the author's view of the fly theory?
o: It has been proved beyond doubt that flies caused zebras to evolve stripes.
It is currently the best supported explanation, although not conclusive.

questions.passage: Students who take notes on a laptop record more words than students writing by hand, and in a well-known study they also performed worse on questions that required them to explain what they had heard. The usual interpretation is that typing is fast enough to allow a transcript, whereas a slow hand forces the writer to summarise, and summarising is itself a form of learning. The finding has been repeated often enough to enter teaching guidance, but it is narrower than it is usually made to sound. Later replications have produced smaller effects, and in several the difference disappeared once students were told to write in their own words rather than transcribe. The medium, in other words, may matter less than the instruction. Handwriting also carries costs that the original study did not weigh: notes cannot be searched, shared or corrected easily, and students with motor or visual difficulties may be excluded altogether. A more defensible conclusion is that the goal is to process material while hearing it, and that any tool which encourages transcription makes that harder.

questions.title: Lecture: the cost of noise
questions.text: When we list environmental threats to health, we usually think of air pollution first. Noise deserves a place on the same list. The World Health Organization estimates that in Western Europe alone, environmental noise costs over a million healthy life years annually, mostly through sleep disturbance and cardiovascular disease. The mechanism is not simply annoyance. Even when a sleeper does not wake, a passing lorry produces a measurable rise in heart rate and stress hormones, and over years this pattern is associated with higher blood pressure. Children are affected differently: studies near airports have found delays in reading development that correlate with aircraft noise at school, and the effect persists after controlling for family income. What makes noise unusual as a pollutant is how cheap the remedies are. Quieter road surfaces, lower night-time speed limits, and simple changes to flight paths deliver measurable benefits at a fraction of the cost of the health effects they prevent. The main obstacle is that noise leaves no residue, so the harm is easy to discount.

questions.text: Before the railways, every town in Britain kept its own time, set by the sun. Oxford was about five minutes behind London, Bristol about ten, and nobody minded, because nobody could travel fast enough for the difference to matter. The railway changed that almost overnight. A timetable printed in London was useless in Bristol if the two cities disagreed about what hour it was, and there were accidents caused by trains on the same line running to different clocks. The Great Western Railway therefore adopted London time across its network in 1840, and other companies followed. For some years many towns kept two times at once: the station clock showed railway time while the town hall showed local time, and some clocks were fitted with two minute hands. Resistance was not trivial, since a town's time was a matter of civic pride, and there were court cases turning on which time a legal deadline referred to. Parliament did not make Greenwich time the legal standard until 1880, forty years after the railways had effectively imposed it. The same pattern repeated internationally. The global system of time zones was agreed at a conference in 1884, and again it was driven by transport and telegraph companies rather than by astronomers, who were quite content with local time for their own purposes.

questions.text: I want to talk today about why so many teenagers are tired, because the usual explanation, that they stay up late by choice, turns out to be only part of the story. At puberty the timing of the body clock shifts later by one to three hours. The hormone that signals the onset of sleep is released later in the evening and clears later in the morning, so a teenager told to go to bed at ten is often being asked to sleep at a time when the body is still alert. This is not a habit acquired from phones; the same shift has been measured in adolescents in communities with no electric light, and it reverses in the early twenties. The practical problem is that school start times have not moved. A number of districts in the United States have now delayed the start of secondary school by an hour, and the results have been consistent: students sleep about thirty minutes longer on average, attendance improves, and road accidents among teenage drivers fall. Test scores rise a little, though less than campaigners hoped. The main obstacles are not educational but logistical, since school buses, sports fixtures and parents' working hours are all built around the existing timetable, and changing one school affects every other.

The deepest cores reach back about eight hundred thousand years, covering eight cycles of glaciation. What the record shows is that carbon dioxide and temperature have moved together, and that today's

questions.text: When a honeybee colony grows too large for its hive, it divides. The old queen leaves with about half the workers, and they gather in a cluster on a branch while scout bees search for a new home. The scouts return and dance to report what they have found, and the length of the dance reflects how good the site is. A scout that has seen a poor site is easily persuaded to go and look at a better one, and over a few hours the dancing converges on a single choice. Only then does the swarm fly. Beekeepers often describe a swarm as a colony in crisis, but it is better understood as reproduction: the colony is making a copy of itself.
questions.q: Which summary best represents the recording?
o: A swarm is how a colony reproduces: scouts report on possible homes by dancing, the colony converges on one site, and only then does it move.
A swarm forms because the colony is starving and its queen has died, which is why beekeepers treat it as an emergency.
Scout bees choose a new home individually, so a swarm usually splits between several sites.

questions.text: Tidal power is more predictable than wind or sunlight, because the tides are set by the moon and can be calculated decades ahead. A tidal barrage across an estuary holds back water at high tide and releases it through turbines as the tide falls. Building a barrage is expensive, the output arrives in four bursts a day rather than continuously, and an estuary is usually a feeding ground for wading birds that a barrage would flood. Recent projects have therefore favoured underwater turbines placed in fast currents, which can be installed in stages and do far less damage to the shore.

questions.text: People are often surprised that a desert which reaches forty degrees in the afternoon can approach freezing before dawn. The reason is not the sand but the air. Water vapour is the main greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, and desert air holds very little of it, so heat radiated by the ground at night escapes to space instead of being absorbed and sent back down. Cloud has the same effect, which is why a cloudy night in any climate is warmer than a clear one. Sand also holds heat poorly compared with soil or rock, so the surface itself cools quickly. Humid regions, by contrast, change temperature slowly, and a tropical coast may vary by only a few degrees between afternoon and dawn.
